lede: One cell becomes two, then four, then a ball. It settles into the wall of the uterus, and only then do its cells start becoming different from one another. Four events, four different kinds of change — and the exam is mostly about telling them apart.
can: Tell a zygote from an embryo, and implantation from differentiation, in one sentence each.
Give the three adaptations of a sperm cell and the reason for each one.
Explain how the placenta is adapted for diffusion, and name what crosses it in each direction.

text: Sperm, fertilisation, implantation and the placenta

md: Between a sperm meeting an ovum and an embryo with tissues in it, four different things happen. Two nuclei fuse. One cell becomes many. The ball moves in somewhere. Only then do its cells become different.

text: 1. The sperm: three parts, three reasons

md:
A sperm is made by **meiosis**, so its nucleus is **haploid**: one chromosome of each pair, half a set.

**Head** — carries that haploid nucleus.
**Middle piece** — packed with **mitochondria**, which release the energy for the swim. *(Higher Tier.)*
**Tail** — the **flagellum**, which makes the sperm **swim** to the ovum.

Saying the tail 'moves' is not the mark. The word the scheme reads for is **swim**.

alt: A scanning electron micrograph of several human sperm cells, showing the rounded head, the short thicker middle piece and the long thin tail of each one.
credit: No specific author, Wikimedia Commons, Public domain
caption: Real sperm under an electron microscope, magnified about three thousand times.
prompt: The tail is many times longer than the head. What does that tell you about where most of the cell's energy goes?
The tail of a sperm cell is called the ______, and its job is to make the sperm ______.
answer: flagellum | flagellum, swim | flagellum and swim
explain: The flagellum, and its job is to make the sperm swim. 'It moves' does not earn the mark; swimming does.

md:
**Fertilisation happens in the oviduct**, not in the uterus. The **haploid** nucleus of the sperm and the **haploid** nucleus of the ovum **fuse**.

Half a set plus half a set makes a whole set, so the single cell that results is **diploid**. That cell is called a **zygote**.

One cell. If you can count the cells and the answer is one, it is a zygote.

prompt: A sperm nucleus and an egg nucleus fuse. What is the single cell that results called?
explain: A zygote: one cell, and diploid. An embryo is what it becomes once it has divided into many cells.

title: Why the ball stays the same size
md:
The zygote divides, and divides again, **without growing in between**. So 2 cells become 4, then 8, then 16 — and after 6 divisions there are 64 — all packed into the space one cell used to fill.

Mitosis makes **identical** cells. Nothing has become anything different yet, and nothing has been added from outside. That is worth holding on to, because it is exactly what changes at the end of this lesson.

title: Words other boards use here
md: The **acrosome**, **blastocyst** (CCEA says *ball of cells*), the **corpus luteum**, **hCG** and the stages of meiosis belong to other specifications, not this one.

prompt: A zygote has divided 5 times by mitosis. How many cells are in the ball?
explain: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. Each division doubles the count, so five divisions give 32 cells.

alt: A microscope image of a human ball of cells a few days after fertilisation: a rounded outer layer of cells with a fluid space inside and a small clump of cells to one side.
credit: Courtesy of NIAID / Ryan Kissinger, Wikimedia Commons, Public domain
caption: A real ball of cells, a few days after fertilisation and about to implant.
prompt: Is this a zygote or an embryo, and how can you tell from the picture alone?

md:
The ball of cells travels down the oviduct and reaches the uterus. **Implantation** is when it sinks into the **lining** of the uterus — the thickened layer inside the wall. The mark scheme wants the word *lining*; 'the uterus' on its own has not been enough.

Only after that do the cells **differentiate**: they become different from one another, making tissues and then organs.

**Implantation is a change of place. Differentiation is a change of job.**

title: Why that last line is in bold
md: Summer 2025's report names the two swaps that cost most marks here: **zygote for embryo**, and **implantation for differentiation**. Place and job is the sentence that separates them.

prompt: The cells in a ball of cells begin to become different from one another, forming tissues. What is this called?
explain: Differentiation — a change of job. Implantation was the change of place that came before it, and mitosis only ever makes identical cells.

title: Worked example: 'Explain how the placenta is adapted for diffusion. [3]'
md:
**Step 1 — recognise the shape.** This is an exchange surface, like the alveolus. The same four points work.
**Step 2 — large surface area.** The **villi** fold it, *so more substances diffuse at once*. **[1]** *(Higher Tier.)*
**Step 3 — thin barrier.** The two blood supplies are separated by a thin layer, *so the distance to diffuse is short*. **[1]**
**Step 4 — good blood supply.** Blood flowing on both sides *keeps the difference in concentration up*. **[1]**

Each mark is a feature **plus** what it achieves. A bare "large surface area" earns nothing.

prompt: Which pair of substances crosses the placenta from the mother's blood into the foetus?
explain: Oxygen and dissolved nutrients go in; carbon dioxide and urea are the wastes that come back out.

text: 6. Cord, amnion, and what the numbers say

title: KS3 Biology - Fertilisation & Pregnancy
why: This clip carries on as far as the placenta, which is where most of this topic's marks are. The uploader labels it KS3 because in England the anatomy is taught earlier, but the content is your B2 content.

md:
The **umbilical cord** carries blood, and everything dissolved in it, to and from the foetus. The **amnion** is the membrane around the foetus, and the **amniotic fluid** inside it **cushions** the foetus. It does not feed it — that is the placenta's job.

The two blood supplies never mix. Glucose falls from 5.4 to 3.6 mmol/dm³ across the placenta, a drop of 33.3%, and that difference is what keeps the diffusion going.

prompt: What is the function of the amniotic fluid around a foetus?
options: it carries oxygen to the foetus
explain: It cushions the foetus. Food and oxygen reach the foetus across the placenta and along the umbilical cord.

md:
Give the three adaptations of a **sperm cell** and the reason for each one.
Say that fertilisation happens in the **oviduct**, and that two haploid nuclei fuse to give a **diploid zygote**.
Tell a **zygote** (one cell) from an **embryo** (many cells), and **implantation** (a change of place, into the **lining**) from **differentiation** (a change of job).
Explain how the **placenta** is adapted, as feature-plus-consequence pairs *(the villi part is Higher Tier)*, and name what crosses it each way.
Give the jobs of the **umbilical cord**, the **amnion** and the **amniotic fluid**.

This content usually carries a whole question of **6 to 9 marks**, walked down as one-mark recall parts: where fertilisation happens, what the single cell is called, what implantation is, what differentiation is. The placenta comes separately as a **[3]** part. Stuck on that one? Write three sentences, each a feature **and a consequence** — a bare feature earns nothing.
